did_you_know.text: Did you know? Amos is introduced as a man from Tekoa, and he prophesied concerning Israel during the reigns of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel.
Did you know? Amos’s prophecy is dated to two years before the earthquake—a quake mentioned here as an event familiar to the people of that time.
Did you know? The opening of the prophecy describes the LORD roaring from Zion and raising his voice from Jerusalem; as a result, the shepherds’ pastures mourn and the top of Carmel dries up.

Did you know? The prophecies against the nations repeatedly use the formula, “For three transgressions of … and for four.” In Damascus, the offense described is threshing Gilead with iron threshing sledges—an image of extreme cruelty in war.
Did you know? Aram’s punishment includes breaking the bar of Damascus and exiling its people to Kir; in this way, the prophecy portrays the downfall of Aram’s power.
Did you know? Gaza is punished for handing over an entire population to Edom. The prophecy also mentions Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron, leading to the destruction of the remnant of the Philistines.

Did you know? Tyre is punished for handing over a population to Edom and for failing to remember a “covenant of brotherhood”—a bond of friendship and treaty cited in the prophecy as an additional reason for judgment.
Did you know? Edom is accused of pursuing its brother with the sword, showing no compassion, and maintaining its anger over time. Teman and Bozrah are mentioned as places where the fire will come.

Did you know? The Ammonites are punished for ripping open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory. The punishment includes striking Rabbah, exiling the king and officials, and a description of a day of warfare and storm.
